caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Ireland's debt arc is the most dramatic recovery in the euro area: 23.7% of GDP in 2006 (the low), exploding to 118.9% in 2012, the series peak, on bank recapitalizations and the property crash, then falling to a projected 32.9% in 2025 (56.9% in 2020, 42.9% in 2022) — the fastest large-scale deleveraging in the EU. GDP soared from $232.2bn in 2006 to a projected $718.1bn in 2025, though multinational accounting inflates the denominator. The state is now running surpluses and building sovereign wealth funds from corporate-tax windfalls; the fiscal question is managing abundance, not solvency.
inflation_management: Irish inflation followed the euro area with a property-bust twist: -1.7% in 2009 (the series low) and -0.5% in 2020 during the adjustment, then 8.1% in 2022, the series high, on energy. It fell to 1.3% in 2024 and is projected at 2.1% for 2025, back near target. Monetary policy is the ECB's; Ireland's distinctive feature is housing-driven services inflation, which has kept underlying pressures firmer than the headline suggests even as energy effects faded.

key_events.event: Property and banking collapse; the state guaranteed bank liabilities (September 2008), socializing the losses.
EU-IMF bailout (November 2010); debt peaked at 118.9% of GDP in 2012.
Exited the bailout (December 2013); rapid export-led recovery began.
Corporate-tax windfalls built surpluses; sovereign wealth funds established.
Energy shock inflation of 8.1%; debt projected at 32.9% of GDP, near pre-crisis levels.

outlook_next_decade: Ireland's outlook is unusually strong but concentrated: corporate-tax receipts fund surpluses and investment, yet the revenue base depends on a handful of multinationals and US tax policy. The housing shortage is the binding domestic constraint, feeding wage and inflation pressure. Debt near 33% of GDP and sovereign wealth funds provide a large buffer. The honest risk assessment: the fiscal position is excellent, but the growth model has a single point of failure in global corporate-tax politics.
